newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK sees opium still casting a shadow over China.
newsitem.headline: HK sees opium still casting a shadow over China.

text.p: Over 150 years after Britain forced opium on China, winning Hong Kong in the bargain, the drug's heroin derivative still casts a shadow over the mainland.

Western officials told Reuters on Thursday that China's 1.2 billion population represents a voracious market not just for consumer goods like automobiles and televisions but for narcotics like heroin and "ice" as well.
"We know that huge quantities of heroin are going into mainland China," said a Western aide with years of experience in the region.
"In a recent year about 200 metric tonnes of heroin were produced in Burma. The main export route used to be by sea but now most of the opium goes overland through China."
"There were only four tonnes of seizures in China that year. While there's no way to prove it, a logical deduction is that most of the balance was consumed internally."
Opium from India was the battering ram Britain used to break down Chinese trade barriers and reverse London's negative balance of payments with Beijing in the mid-19th century.
When China resisted, capturing and destroying 20,000 chests of British opium in the process, war resulted.
China lost the opium war and Hong Kong, a humiliation to be rectified at midnight on June 30 when the territory reverts to Beijing.
Opium dens where smokers inhale pipes prepared by attendants are largely a thing of the past but China's appetite for heroin and methamphetamines, known as 'ice', remains enormous.
The plant Ephedra Equisetina grows in the south of China in abundance. It provides the base for ephedrine, which in turn is used in the production of methamphetamines like ice.
Relatively cheap and powerful, methamphetamines are consumed in China's teeming urban centres and exported to other Asian destinations including the Philippines and Australia.
Western officials say that despite China's internal drug problem, the handover of Hong Kong from Britain to China is not expected to complicate narcotics enforcement.
This despite the fact that Chinese gangs known as Triads are active in all kinds of illicit dealings in Hong Kong and south China.
"The handover can only make our lives easier since we expect our contacts and cooperation with China on drugs, which is minimal now, to grow," said one Western official.
"The Hong Kong police are among the most professional in the world and they are very well paid, which reduces the opportunity for bribes and corruption."
"China's penalties against drug traffickers (often including the death sentence) are severe. The handover is a good thing for drug enforcement from our point of view."
